rep.summary:
I audited the upscaling path on branch beta of <repo> and changed nothing.

**Which FSR it is.** The emulator ships AMD FidelityFX Super Resolution 1 ("FSR 1", header version v1.20210629, the original June 2021 release). FSR 1 is a purely spatial upscaler. There is no FSR 2, 3 or 4 code, and nothing temporal (no motion vectors, no history).

**Which parts are used.** Only two passes run, both using the 16-bit (FP16, A_HALF) shader path, with no 32-bit fallback:
- EASU (the upscaling pass, FsrEasuH)
- RCAS (the sharpening pass, FsrRcasH)

The optional helpers in the header (LFGA film grain, SRTM tone mapper, TEPD dither, FSR_RCAS_DENOISE) are present but never used.

**When FSR runs.** FsrPass::Render only runs when FSR is enabled and the game's video-out buffer is smaller than the presentation frame in at least one dimension. The presentation frame is the window's game area, aspect-fitted. If the input is equal or larger, FSR is skipped and the post-process pass simply stretches or shrinks the image with a bilinear (linear) sampler. RCAS sharpening only ever runs inside the FSR branch, so nothing is sharpened when there is no upscaling.

**Bug: RCAS sharpening does nothing.** The launcher stores attenuation as a whole number in thousandths (default 250, meaning 0.25 stops). fsr_pass.cpp:278 passes that raw number to FsrRcasCon instead of the value divided by 1000.
- Sharpness then becomes 2^-250, which is zero in 16-bit, so RCAS returns the input pixel unchanged.
- The correctly scaled value (`settings.rcasAttenuation`) is computed in vk_presenter.cpp:491/502 and by the live-update path from the launcher (`SET_RCAS_ATTENUATION`), but FsrPass never reads it.
- So the "Enable RCAS" checkbox and the attenuation slider have no visible effect today.

**Effect for UFC players.** The video-out buffer is 1920x1080 (the game composites its 3D scene and UI into it).
- 1080p fullscreen or any smaller window (default window is 1280x720): FSR is skipped. Display is 1:1 or a bilinear downscale, with no sharpening.
- 1440p or 4K window: FSR 1 EASU upscales the already-finished 1080p image, UI included. It adds no new detail. Sharpening is missing because of the bug above.

**FSR and the render-resolution setting are unrelated.** FSR never touches the game's internal 3D resolution (default 1600x900). ApplyRenderResolution only rewrites the game's width/height constants. The game then scales that 3D image up to its 1080p output with its own shader, before the emulator ever sees the frame.

**Launcher already has lower resolutions.** On this branch the launcher's render-resolution list (settings_dialog.cpp:124-135, commit ab79153) already offers:
- Game default (1600x900)
- 640x360, 768x432, 960x540 and 1024x576, marked "experimental"
- 1280x720, 1920x1080, 2560x1440 and 3840x2160

It applies to UFC 4 (CUSA14204, CUSA14209) and UFC 3 (CUSA06534) only.

**XeSS feasibility.** At the presenter the emulator only has the final colour image (alpha forced to 1). There is no depth buffer, no motion vectors, no camera jitter, and the UI is already baked in.
- XeSS Super Resolution is temporal. Intel's guide says it replaces the game's TAA stage and needs jitter, motion vectors and the low-resolution frame. So it cannot run on that image in any meaningful way. FSR 2/3/4 and DLSS have the same requirement.
- The only other hook point is the rasterizer/texture cache (the game's 1600x900 scene and depth buffers). Even there:
  - nothing marks which buffer is the scene before the UI is drawn
  - there are no motion vectors unless UFC renders its own
  - jitter would have to be injected into the game's projection maths
  - the game's own later passes would have to be redirected to a buffer of a different size
- XeSS is also distributed as a binary-only library under Intel's license (no modification or reverse engineering allowed), which is a likely conflict with shadPS4's GPL-2.0-or-later. That last point is my inference, not legal advice.

**Practical alternatives.** Low internal resolution plus a better spatial upscaler or sharpener is what fits here. The cheapest real improvement is fixing the RCAS scaling so sharpening works again. Running FSR 1/RCAS (or CAS, a similar sharpening filter) at 1:1 when there is no upscaling would also help, as it would sharpen the game's own blurry 900p/720p→1080p upscale.

**Smaller issues found:**
- With an HDR swapchain the FSR shader squares the output colour (`Sample.x == 1` → `c *= c`), which looks wrong for PQ-encoded input. This is an inference I have not tested.
- For 8-bit sRGB video-out formats, EASU runs on linear-decoded data, while AMD's notes ask for sRGB/gamma-like input.
- `Presenter::IsVideoOutSurface` is dead code.
- EmulatorSettings has a duplicate set of FSR defaults (fsr_enabled false) that nothing reads; the active Config default is FSR on.

facts.claim: The vendored FSR is FidelityFX Super Resolution 1 ('FSR 1 ... SPATIAL SCALING & EXTRAS - v1.20210629'); ffx_a.h is 'SHADER PORTABILITY 1.20210629'. No FSR2/3/4 sources exist in the tree (only ffx_a.h and ffx_fsr1.h in host_shaders/fsr).
fsr.comp is compiled twice: as fsr_easu_comp (SAMPLE_EASU=1) and fsr_rcas_comp (SAMPLE_RCAS=1), with --target-env vulkan1.3.

fsr.comp defines A_HALF and uses only the FP16 functions FsrEasuH and FsrRcasH (EASU input via textureGather, RCAS via texelFetch). It does not use the FP32 *F variants, packed Hx2, LFGA, SRTM, TEPD or FSR_RCAS_DENOISE. A_HALF makes the shader require GL_EXT_shader_16bit_storage and GL_EXT_shader_explicit_arithmetic_types; there is no FP32 fallback.

FsrPass::Render returns the input unchanged (FSR off) if settings.enable is false, or if input_size.width >= output_size.width AND input_size.height >= output_size.height. It only runs when the output is larger than the input in at least one dimension.
RCAS only runs inside the FSR branch (EASU into an intermediate image, then RCAS into the output). When FSR is skipped there is no sharpening at all. With use_rcas=false only EASU runs.

BUG: the RCAS constant is built from the raw config integer: FsrRcasCon(..., Config::getRcasAttenuation()). The config stores thousandths (default 250 = 0.25 stops; slider 0..3000 shown as value/1000). FsrRcasCon computes sharpness = exp2(-sharpness), so 2^-250 underflows to 0 in the FP16 constant. In FsrRcasH, lobe *= con.y gives lobe = 0, so the output equals the centre pixel. RCAS is effectively a no-op at every slider setting except 0.

The correctly scaled value settings.rcasAttenuation (= getRcasAttenuation()/1000) is computed by the presenter and by the IPC command SET_RCAS_ATTENUATION, but FsrPass never reads settings.rcasAttenuation.

FSR input is the guest video-out buffer from the texture cache (FindImage on the VideoOut BufferAttributeGroup), at the guest buffer size image.info.size, viewed with alpha swizzled to ONE. Output size is {frame->width, frame->height}.

Frame size = the ImGui 'Display' window content area, aspect-fitted to the video-out aspect (SetExpectedGameSize). The frame is then drawn 1:1 into the swapchain with ImGui::Image. In practice the output size is the window or fullscreen client size, letterboxed. The default window is 1280x720.
FSR intermediate and output images are RGBA16F at output size, one pair per swapchain image.

HDR handling: when the swapchain is HDR, Sample.x=1 and the last FSR pass squares the colour (c *= c). This is the gamma-2.0-to-linear convention from AMD's sample. The post-process pass passes colour through unchanged when hdr is set.

Squaring the colour in HDR mode is probably wrong for PQ (A2R10G10B10Bt2020Pq) video-out, which is sampled as UNORM. It would likely darken or shift HDR output when FSR is active. Not tested; UFC is probably not HDR.

For 8-bit sRGB video-out formats the view is R8G8B8A8Srgb/B8G8R8A8Srgb, so EASU samples linear-decoded values. The FSR1 header asks for input whose 'tonemapping curve needs to be as if presenting to sRGB display (e.g. Gamma 2.0)'. It also says EASU is best applied 'before film grain or composite of the UI'; here the UI is already composited.

The post-process pass always runs. It draws a full-screen triangle at frame size, sampling the FSR output or the raw video-out with a LINEAR sampler (clamp to edge, no mips). So any non-FSR scaling (downscale to a smaller window, or upscale when FSR is off) is plain bilinear. It also applies the gamma slider and sRGB decode for A2R10G10B10Srgb. No nearest-neighbour or integer-scaling option exists.

Default settings in the active Config: fsrEnabled=true, rcasEnabled=true, rcasAttenuation=250 (0.25). EmulatorSettings has a separate fsr_enabled{false} default, but its getters are not referenced anywhere.

The launcher exposes these on the Graphics tab: 'Enable FSR' and 'Enable RCAS (sharpening)' checkboxes, plus an RCAS Attenuation slider (0..3000) with a spin box (0.000..3.000). They are pushed live to a running game over IPC (SET_FSR, SET_RCAS, SET_RCAS_ATTENUATION). Tooltip: 'FSR upscales the game picture to the window size ... It does not change the resolution the game renders at.' The per-game dialog has the same controls.
The devtools frame graph shows 'Game Res', 'Output Res' and 'FSR: on/off' (DebugState.is_using_fsr). Players can check whether FSR actually ran.

1080p monitor, fullscreen, video-out 1920x1080: input equals output, so FSR is skipped and the image is shown 1:1 with no sharpening. Any smaller window: FSR skipped, bilinear downscale. 1440p/4K: EASU upscales the finished 1080p frame (UI included); RCAS has no effect because of the attenuation bug.

The render-resolution patch is independent of FSR. ApplyRenderResolution only overwrites the immediate 1600/900 constants in the game's resolution setup (UFC 4 CUSA14204/CUSA14209, UFC 3 CUSA06534; SHADPS4_RENDER_RES env var overrides), and is called at module load. The game itself scales the 3D scene into its 1080p video-out buffer, so FSR sees the same 1920x1080 input whatever the internal resolution.
That the video-out buffer stays 1920x1080 and the game does its own upscale of the 3D scene is taken from the task description and the launcher tooltip. I did not check it against a run log.

The launcher already offers render resolutions below 900p: 'Game default (1600x900)', 640x360/768x432/960x540/1024x576 (marked experimental), and 1280x720, plus 1080p/1440p/4K. Added in commit ab79153.
Only final colour is available at the presenter: one RGB image (alpha forced to 1), with UI already composited. No depth, motion vectors, jitter or exposure reach the presenter.

A scene-only hook would have to live in the rasterizer and texture cache: BeginRendering/FindRenderTarget/FindDepthTarget bind every guest colour and depth target. Presenter::IsVideoOutSurface exists but is unused (dead code). Nothing tags which target is the 3D scene before the UI is drawn, or where the game's own upscale happens.

XeSS Super Resolution is temporal: it replaces the engine's TAA stage and needs jittered low-resolution colour, motion vectors and a jitter offset. Exposure is optional (autoexposure flag). Whether depth is mandatory was not confirmed.

XeSS SDK 2.0.1 introduced Vulkan 1.1 support for XeSS-SR. It runs on Intel Iris Xe or later, and on other vendors' GPUs that support shaderIntegerDotProduct, shaderStorageReadWithoutFormat and mutableDescriptorType. The current SDK is branded 'XeSS 3'; XeSS-SR supports GPUs with SM 6.4 (DP4a).

The XeSS SDK is under the Intel Simplified Software License: 'provided in binary form only', with no modification and no reverse engineering. This probably conflicts with shadPS4's GPL-2.0-or-later licence (inference, not legal advice). I found no documented Linux support.

rep.implications:
1) FSR is FSR 1 (spatial, FP16 EASU + RCAS). On the most common UFC setup (1080p screen, 1920x1080 video-out, or the default 1280x720 window) it does nothing: the pass is skipped and the image is shown 1:1 or downscaled bilinearly. It only upscales the finished 1080p frame on 1440p/4K displays. Even then sharpening does nothing, because fsr_pass.cpp:278 passes 250 instead of 0.25 to FsrRcasCon. One-line fix: use settings.rcasAttenuation, which the presenter and IPC already scale by 1/1000.

2) The render-resolution setting and FSR never interact. Lowering UFC's internal resolution (720p and below already exist in the launcher, settings_dialog.cpp:124-135) is upscaled by the game's own shader to 1080p, with no help from FSR.

3) The most useful improvement for weak PCs would be a 1:1 sharpening option on the presented frame: RCAS/CAS also when input == output, after fixing the attenuation bug. It would counter the blur of the game's 900p/720p→1080p upscale. It is cheap and needs no engine data. Optionally, offer FSR 1 EASU for windows smaller than 1080p instead of bilinear.

4) XeSS (and FSR 2/3/4, DLSS) is not realistically feasible:
- The presenter only has final colour, with the UI already composited: no depth, no motion vectors, no jitter.
- A scene-level hook in the rasterizer/texture cache would need per-game reverse engineering:
  - identify the scene colour and depth targets
  - inject sub-pixel jitter into the game's projection
  - get or generate motion vectors
  - make the game's later passes accept a buffer of a different size
- XeSS is a binary-only proprietary library, which likely conflicts with the GPL licence of shadPS4.
- A spatial-only use of XeSS (no motion vectors) is not what the SDK is designed for. Expect little benefit over FSR 1 plus working RCAS.

5) Minor follow-ups:
- HDR + FSR squares PQ-encoded values (likely a colour bug; untested).
- EASU runs on linear-decoded sRGB data, while AMD's notes ask for sRGB/gamma-like input.
- The FP16-only shader has no FP32 fallback for GPUs without shaderFloat16 (Intel Arc, recent NVIDIA and AMD iGPUs support it).
- Presenter::IsVideoOutSurface and EmulatorSettings' FSR defaults are dead code.

checks.claim: The vendored FSR is FSR 1 v1.20210629 (ffx_fsr1.h:5, ffx_a.h:4). Only ffx_a.h and ffx_fsr1.h are in host_shaders/fsr; there is no FSR 2/3/4.
fsr.comp is compiled twice (SAMPLE_EASU / SAMPLE_RCAS) with --target-env vulkan1.3.
fsr.comp defines A_HALF and uses only FsrEasuH/FsrRcasH (textureGather / texelFetch). No FP32, LFGA, SRTM, TEPD or denoise. A_HALF requires the 16-bit extensions, with no FP32 fallback.
checks.correction: Minor addition: vk_instance only enables shaderFloat16 and 16-bit storage when the device reports them. A GPU without FP16 would therefore get an invalid FSR pipeline. Not a concern for Arc, recent NVIDIA or AMD iGPUs.

checks.claim: FsrPass::Render returns the input if FSR is disabled, or if input >= output in both dimensions.
RCAS runs only inside the FSR branch (EASU into an intermediate image, then RCAS). With use_rcas=false only EASU runs.
BUG: line 278 passes the raw integer (default 250) to FsrRcasCon. 2^-250 becomes 0, so RCAS outputs the centre pixel. RCAS is a no-op at every slider setting except 0.
checks.correction: The bug is real; only the 'every setting except 0' part is wrong. FsrRcasCon computes exp2(-N) with N = the raw integer, and the CPU half converter keeps fp16 subnormals down to 2^-24 (ffx_a.h:483-508). So raw values 0..~24 (shown as 0.000..0.024 in the launcher) still sharpen: 0 = maximum, 1 = 1 stop, 2 = 2 stops, and so on. Anything above ~24, including the default 250, gives exactly zero sharpening. Players can get sharpening today by setting the value to 0.000-0.003. The bug is fork-specific: upstream shadps4-emu passes settings.rcas_attenuation (already divided by 1000). The line arrived with the fork's base commit 9032654 (git blame).

checks.claim: settings.rcasAttenuation (value/1000) is computed by the presenter and by IPC SET_RCAS_ATTENUATION, but FsrPass never reads it.
checks.correction: Addition: there are two IPC handlers with the same behaviour (src/qt_gui/main.cpp:539-543 and src/core/ipc/ipc.cpp:169-174). So the launcher's live slider updates for a running game have no effect at all. The reverse mismatch also exists. The in-game devtools 'FSR Enabled' and 'RCAS' checkboxes write only to Config (layer.cpp:1238-1245), but FsrPass reads settings.enable and settings.use_rcas, which nothing refreshes from that path. Those two toggles therefore do not apply live. The devtools 'Sharpness' slider writes to Config, which line 278 reads, so it is the only live control of RCAS strength, and only near 0.

checks.claim: FSR input is the video-out image from the texture cache, at image.info.size, with alpha swizzled to ONE. Output is {frame->width, frame->height}.
Frame size is the Display window's content area, aspect-fitted (SetExpectedGameSize). The default window is 1280x720.
The FSR intermediate and output images are RGBA16F at output size, one pair per swapchain image.
In HDR mode the last FSR pass squares the colour, and the post-process pass passes colour through unchanged.
checks.correction: Precision: EASU squares only when RCAS is off (Sample = hdr && !use_rcas); otherwise RCAS squares. pp_settings.hdr is set by SetHDR.

checks.claim: Squaring the colour is probably wrong for PQ video-out (inference, untested).
checks.correction: This is a reasonable inference and is labelled as one. PQ is sampled through an A2R10G10B10 UNORM view (vk_presenter.cpp:657-659).

checks.claim: For 8-bit sRGB formats EASU runs on linear-decoded data, while the FSR1 header wants gamma-like input before the UI is composited.
checks.correction: Addition: for A2R10G10B10Srgb the view is UNORM, so EASU sees gamma-encoded data (correct for FSR), and the decode happens later in post_process.frag:41.

checks.claim: The post-process pass always runs with a LINEAR, clamp-to-edge, non-mipmapped sampler. All non-FSR scaling is bilinear, and there is no nearest-neighbour or integer-scale option.
checks.correction: Note: with no mips, a downscale below 0.5x will alias.

checks.claim: Active Config defaults are fsrEnabled=true, rcasEnabled=true, rcasAttenuation=250. The EmulatorSettings fsr_enabled{false} is unused.
checks.correction: No Get*Fsr/Rcas EmulatorSettings getter call sites were found outside emulator_settings.h.

The devtools frame graph shows Game Res, Output Res and FSR on/off.

checks.correction: Detail: for UFC 3 the patched code picks 1920x1080 or 1600x900 via cmovne, and only the 1600x900 pair is replaced. If the game takes the 1080p branch (e.g. PS4 Pro/neo mode), the setting may do nothing. That is an inference from the pattern comment. Accepted range is 64..3840 x 64..2160.

checks.correction: This is correctly labelled as unverified. The devtools 'Game Res' line (frame_graph.cpp:107) would confirm it in one run.

checks.claim: XeSS-SR is temporal: it replaces TAA and needs jitter, colour and motion vectors. Exposure is optional. Whether depth is mandatory was not confirmed.
checks.correction: The depth question can be answered from the current guide. The minimum inputs are jitter, colour and dilated high-res motion vectors, or alternatively undilated low-res motion vectors plus depth (the default mode). Depth is required unless the integrator supplies dilated high-res motion vectors. For LDR input, Intel recommends exposure = 1.0 and no auto-exposure.

checks.claim: XeSS 2.0.1 introduced Vulkan 1.1 support for XeSS-SR (Iris Xe or later, or other vendors with shaderIntegerDotProduct, shaderStorageReadWithoutFormat and mutableDescriptorType). The SDK is now 'XeSS 3', and XeSS-SR needs SM 6.4/DP4a.
checks.correction: The release note matches. The current developer guide lists the non-Intel Vulkan requirements as shaderStorageImageWriteWithoutFormat and mutableDescriptorType, and says to query the needed extensions and features through SDK functions.

checks.claim: XeSS uses the Intel Simplified Software License (binary only, no modification, no reverse engineering), which probably conflicts with GPL-2.0-or-later. No documented Linux support was found.
checks.correction: License text verified (Version October 2022). The Linux point is stronger than 'not found': the guide's requirements list Windows 10/11 x64 only, and deployment is libxess.dll plus the MSVC redistributable. That is fine for the Windows players but rules out the Linux build. The GPL point remains an inference, not legal advice.

checks.claim: Implication: offer FSR 1 EASU instead of bilinear for windows smaller than 1080p.
checks.correction: EASU is designed for upscaling: its constants describe input-to-output scaling, and AMD documents it as an upscaler. Using it for downscaling is not a supported mode and would bring little benefit. A proper downscale filter or mipmapped sampling would be the right tool there. This is an inference from the FSR 1 design.

chk.missing:
1) Lower render resolutions: the report says the launcher 'already' has 720p and below. It omits that 1280x720 existed since 1a54440 (2026-10-13), while 640x360, 768x432, 960x540 and 1024x576 were added today (2026-10-15) by this same Claude session in ab79153. That commit is already on origin/beta and has not been tested in UFC 3 or UFC 4. The owner should be told this plainly, and someone should run one test to check that menus and effects survive at 960x540 and 640x360.

2) Which FSR works and how: there is a live workaround the report missed. Because of the scaling bug, an RCAS attenuation of 0.000-0.003 in the launcher gives strong sharpening right now. The default 0.250 gives none. The fix is one line: replace Config::getRcasAttenuation() with settings.rcasAttenuation in fsr_pass.cpp:278, which is what upstream shadPS4 does. Live updates are also inconsistent:
- The launcher IPC slider changes a value FsrPass never reads.
- The in-game devtools FSR/RCAS checkboxes write Config, which FsrPass does not read for enable/use_rcas.

3) A practical way to make FSR useful for weak PCs, which the report missed: FSR 1 only helps if the video-out buffer itself is smaller than the window. Lowering only the 3D resolution means the game upscales with its own (bilinear-like) shader and FSR never sees a low-resolution frame. Two options:
- Patch the game's video-out/backbuffer size too (e.g. 1280x720 video-out). The emulator's EASU+RCAS would then do the upscale, with the UI also rendered at low resolution.
- Keep 1080p video-out and add a 1:1 CAS/RCAS pass.

Both are inferences that need per-game testing. The devtools 'Game Res' readout (frame_graph.cpp:107) would confirm the actual video-out size in one run, which the report left unverified.

4) Temporal alternatives and licences: FSR 2 is MIT-licensed open source with an official Vulkan backend (https://github.com/GPUOpen-Effects/FidelityFX-FSR2). It is GPL-compatible, unlike XeSS, but needs the same inputs (depth, motion vectors, jitter applied to all rendering), so it is blocked for the same reason. The current FidelityFX SDK lists FSR 2.3.4, FSR 3.1.5 and FSR 4.1.1 (ML), and its known issues say 'Vulkan is currently not supported in SDK' (https://github.com/GPUOpen-LibrariesAndSDKs/FidelityFX-SDK). So the licence is not the only blocker for XeSS: any temporal upscaler is blocked by missing engine data, and newer AMD SDKs are not a Vulkan drop-in either.

5) XeSS specifics: depth is required in the default low-res-motion-vector mode. XeSS-SR officially supports Windows 10/11 only. Intel asks that all XeSS settings be exposed to users. Driver-side XeSS overrides (as with OptiScaler-style tools) do not apply here, because the PS4 game makes no XeSS/DLSS/FSR2 calls to intercept. That last point is an inference.

rep.summary: Adding XeSS to this emulator is technically possible on Windows, but it would be a poor fit and is hard to justify on licensing grounds. The latest SDK is XeSS SDK 3.0.2 (2026-07-23), and its repo at https://github.com/intel/xess was last updated 2026-09-09. Vulkan support for super resolution (XeSS-SR) first appeared in SDK 2.0.1 (March 2025) and is still there in 3.x. On Vulkan only XeSS-SR is available: frame generation (XeSS-FG), multi-frame generation and Xe Low Latency (XeLL) are DirectX 12 only. XeSS-SR is purely temporal. Every frame it needs a jittered colour image, motion vectors, a sub-pixel jitter offset, and either a depth buffer or full-resolution motion vectors. There is no spatial mode without motion vectors. The closest built-in option is the 'AA' preset (1.0x scale), which is still temporal. The SDK ships only as Windows DLLs (libxess.dll is about 78 MB) under the 'Intel Simplified Software License': you may redistribute it unmodified, but you may not reverse-engineer it or modify it 'or its operation at any time, including during execution'. Only the public headers became MIT in 2026-09. Linking a GPL-2.0-or-later program like shadPS4 to this non-free library would need a GPL linking exception from all copyright holders. Loading the DLL at runtime only if the user supplies it is the usual workaround, and its legal status is uncertain. No major open-source emulator ships XeSS. My checks of the RPCS3, Ryujinx (Ryubing), xenia-canary, PCSX2, Dolphin and shadPS4 upstream repos found no XeSS code (the PCSX2 hits were false matches on 'FixesSettings'); I did not check yuzu forks hosted off GitHub. The open-source projects that do integrate XeSS through Vulkan are renderers that produce their own motion vectors and jitter, such as NVIDIA dxvk-remix. Wrappers either reuse the motion vectors and depth of a game that already supports DLSS, FSR2 or XeSS (OptiScaler) or work on the final image. Those final-image tools are either spatial upscalers (Lossless Scaling, Magpie) or feed XeSS zero or estimated motion vectors (an experimental Magpie fork), which gives ghosting or artifacts. For context, the emulator's existing FSR is FSR 1 (EASU upscale plus RCAS sharpening), which is spatial only.

rep.implications:
1) XeSS cannot be dropped into the presenter the way FSR1 was. At the presenter the emulator has only the final video-out image, with the 3D scene and UI already merged. It has no motion vectors, depth or jitter. XeSS-SR requires jitter plus motion vectors plus depth (or full-resolution motion vectors), and has no spatial mode. Running it on the final image with zero motion vectors, as the experimental Magpie fork does, gives a ghosting, UI-smearing temporal filter, or roughly no benefit on a static camera. Fighting games like UFC have fast character motion and a lot of HUD, so that would look worse than the current FSR1 at the same input resolution.
2) The only route to good quality is per-game engine work: find UFC 3/4's own velocity and depth buffers (if the engine writes them), inject sub-pixel jitter into the game's projection through the shader recompiler, pass in the internal 3D scene before UI composition, then composite the UI. That is deep, fragile and specific to each game; the bloodborne_pc project describes the same approach for FSR 3, DLSS and XeSS and has not shipped it. It is not realistic for this fork.
3) Platform and licensing: the SDK is Windows-only and binary-only, and its licence bans 'modification ... of its operation ... including during execution'. Shipping it with a GPL-2.0-or-later emulator conflicts with the GPL unless all copyright holders add a linking exception. At most, the emulator could load a DLL the user supplies, and the legal position of that is still uncertain. No major open-source emulator ships XeSS.
4) For players on weak PCs (Intel Arc, NVIDIA, AMD iGPU), the practical options are: lower the internal 3D resolution with the existing per-game patch (for example 1280x720 or 960x540) and keep FSR1 EASU+RCAS for spatial upscaling. FSR1 is already present and needs no motion vectors, so it should be checked that it actually runs when enabled. Optionally add other spatial or sharpening filters, such as AMD CAS or NVIDIA NIS, both open source. Players who want frame generation can use Lossless Scaling on the emulator window on Windows. On Intel Arc, XeSS would at best work like a temporal anti-aliaser, not a real upscaler, unless the per-game motion-vector work in point 2 is done.

FsrRcasCon reads its argument as a number of stops and computes sharpness = exp2(-x) (ffx_fsr1.h:663-668). The default therefore gives 2^-250, which is about 0, so there is no sharpening; only slider value 0 sharpens. Upstream passes the float `settings.rcas_attenuation` (upstream fsr_pass.cpp:275). In this fork, fsr_settings.rcasAttenuation is computed (vk_presenter.cpp:491, 502; settings_dialog.cpp:2071, 2083) but never used in Render. Answer to 'does FSR work': EASU works, RCAS currently does almost nothing.

2) When FSR runs at all: it is on by default (config.cpp:291), but it runs only when the presenter frame (window content area, or fullscreen size, with the aspect ratio kept) is larger than the game's video-out buffer (fsr_pass.cpp:142). It works on the final composited image, UI included. DebugState.is_using_fsr (fsr_pass.cpp:139-147) shows whether it is active. With a 1080p video-out buffer on a 1080p screen, FSR does nothing.

3) The FSR1 work-around in the report does not hold (see the implication-4 check above). FSR never touches the reduced internal 3D render; the game itself scales the 3D scene into the video-out buffer.

4) Scope of the per-game render-resolution patch: it covers only UFC 4 CUSA14204 and CUSA14209 and UFC 3 CUSA06534 (EU). Other UFC 3 regions are not covered (memory_patcher.cpp:706-717). The header comment memory_patcher.h:48 still says 'UFC 4' only. The checked-out HEAD ab79153 already adds 1024x576, 960x540, 768x432 and 640x360 (marked experimental) to the launcher list, and the patch accepts sizes from 64x64 upward. This bears on the owner's first question.

5) XeSS is a poor match for the target hardware even apart from the missing inputs. Intel recommends XeSS Balanced only at 1080p output and above, and Performance or Ultra Performance only at 1440p and above (dev guide lines 186-195). Non-Intel GPUs are recommended from RTX 3000 / RX 6000. Weak PCs with AMD Vega-class iGPUs or GTX cards fall below that, and the DP4a pass costs fixed milliseconds at output resolution. This is an inference; I have no benchmarks.

6) Better route if temporal upscaling is ever attempted: AMD FSR 2 / FSR 3.1 is open source (MIT) and has Vulkan backends, so it fits GPL-2.0-or-later with no licence problem. Its inputs (colour, depth, motion vectors, jitter, scene before UI) are the same ones XeSS needs. bbport did exactly this: 'DLSS gets the inputs FSR 3.1 gets'. So the per-game engine work could target FSR 3.1 first, with XeSS as an optional backend that loads a DLL the user supplies. The report misses that bbport shipped this approach (FSR 3.1, FSR 4, DLSS) in a shadPS4-derived renderer by computing motion vectors and Halton jitter itself for a game with no velocity buffer. That is real evidence the work is feasible, though heavy and game-specific (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/deadinside28/bloodborne_pc/master/README.md).

7) XeSS-SR must replace the game's own TAA, take linear pre-UI colour, and needs a texture mip bias adjusted to the scale factor (dev guide lines 86-98, 197-198). An emulator would have to find and disable the UFC engine's TAA or post-AA pass and apply the LOD bias in its own samplers. Both are game-specific; this is an inference from the guide.

8) Cheaper spatial options to consider: AMD CAS (MIT) and Snapdragon GSR (BSD-3). These are suggestions only; I did not verify their licences in this session.

rep.summary:
This report answers both parts of the request with web and source research. Facts checked directly against a primary source are marked "verified". Conclusions I drew myself are labelled as inferences.

**(1) FSR in the emulator.** Upstream shadPS4 (shadps4-emu/shadPS4 main @ b2d7ec7d) and this fork both ship AMD FSR 1. It is the MIT-licensed EASU+RCAS code, run as two GLSL compute passes in the Vulkan presenter. Neither has FSR 2, 3 or 4.

The FSR 1 pass only does anything when the game's video-out image is smaller than the window or swapchain. The early-out is at local src/video_core/renderer_vulkan/host_passes/fsr_pass.cpp:142 (upstream line 139). In practice:
- A UFC game with a 1080p video-out buffer on a 1080p window gets no FSR at all.
- On a 1440p or 4K display it upscales the whole composited frame, UI included.

**(2) XeSS is not realistic.** XeSS-SR is a temporal upscaler. It needs jitter, colour and motion vectors every frame (or low-res motion vectors plus depth). It is shipped as a binary-only Windows DLL under the Intel Simplified Software License, which forbids modification. The emulator has no reliable motion vectors or jitter. FSR 2/3/4, DLSS and SGSR 2 hit the same wall: they all need depth, motion vectors and camera jitter. FSR 4 also needs an RX 9000-series GPU, DX12/HLSL SM6.4 and signed binaries.

**Options an emulator that only has the final colour image can actually use.** All are permissive, shader-source spatial filters:
- **FSR 1 (EASU+RCAS)**, MIT. Already integrated here.
- **AMD CAS**, MIT. A sharpener with optional limited upscale. Works at 1:1 scale.
- **NVIDIA Image Scaling (NIS)**, MIT, v1.0.3. One compute pass, with GLSL and HLSL shaders. Quality is about the same as FSR 1; the main difference is that its default sharpening is stronger.
- **Qualcomm SGSR 1**, BSD-3. A single-pass Lanczos-like filter plus sharpening. Quality is "on par" with other spatial upscalers, and it is cheaper than the two-pass FSR 1. Eden and ARMSX2 already ship it.

**What other emulators ship.** RPCS3, Xenia, Vita3K, yuzu (and Eden), Ryujinx, PPSSPP and shadPS4 all ship FSR 1. Xenia also ships CAS, and Eden also ships SGSR. Dolphin and Cemu ship classic resampling filters only. RPCS3 states the reason publicly: there are no per-object motion vectors, so only spatial methods fit.

**Driver-level and external options players can use today without emulator changes:**
- **AMD RSR**: FSR 1 in the driver. It needs desktop systems with a discrete RX 5000 or newer, or select AMD Advantage systems, so AMD iGPUs are mostly excluded. It works in exclusive or borderless fullscreen and only activates when the game resolution is below native.
- **NVIDIA NIS (driver)**: needs fullscreen at a lower-than-native resolution, or a lowered desktop resolution.
- **Intel**: no universal spatial upscaler in the driver, only retro/integer scaling. The XeSS override applies only to games that already integrate XeSS 2.
- **Lossless Scaling**: about $7 on Steam, closed source. Offers LS1, FSR, NIS and frame generation (LSFG). Needs windowed or borderless mode. This is the only universal option on Intel Arc.
- **Windows Auto SR**: does not apply. It does not support Vulkan, and it needs a Copilot+ PC (Snapdragon X or Intel Core Ultra Series 3) or the ROG Xbox Ally X.

**Verdict on "render lower in the presenter + spatial upscale".** It would not lower GPU load for UFC. The guest's GPU work is set by the game's own render targets: the 3D scene at 1600x900 by default, plus UI composited into the 1080p video-out buffer. The presenter only resamples that finished image, and its cost is small (AMD's figures are well under a millisecond on desktop GPUs).

Making the presenter or swapchain smaller saves almost nothing and loses detail. The real lever is the existing per-game internal-resolution patch:
- 1600x900 to 1280x720 cuts about 36% of the 3D pixels.
- 1600x900 to 960x540 cuts about 64%.

The emulator's upscaler only helps in two cases:
- **a)** The video-out buffer itself is made smaller than the window. FSR 1 then engages automatically.
- **b)** A sharpen-only pass (CAS or RCAS at 1:1) is added when input is greater than or equal to output. This restores some crispness after the game's own low-res-to-1080p upscale; Xenia does exactly this.

A sharpen-only pass is cheap and easy to add. Adding SGSR 1 or NIS alongside FSR 1 is optional; they cost a little less but are not clearly better. A temporal method (XeSS, FSR 2+) would require finding the game's own pre-upscale render target, depth and motion vectors inside the guest's GPU commands, for each title. That is impractical.

The local presenter feeds FSR with the guest image size as input and the frame (swapchain) size as output, after capturing the guest output, then runs the post-process pass.
FSR support arrived in shadPS4 v0.7.0 (March 2025).

FSR 1 is MIT-licensed spatial upscaling (EASU) plus sharpening (RCAS). It needs only an already anti-aliased colour frame and no history or motion vectors. Presets: 1.3x/1.5x/1.7x/2.0x per axis. Cost is under 0.5 ms at 1440p on an RX 5700 XT or RTX 2060 Super class GPU (under 1 ms at 4K). It should run after tonemapping.
AMD CAS is MIT-licensed, 'a low overhead adaptive sharpening algorithm with optional up-sampling' (Timothy Lottes).

NVIDIA Image Scaling SDK v1.0.3 is MIT-licensed. It ships NIS_Scaler.h (HLSL) plus NIS_Main.hlsl and NIS_Main.glsl, and runs as a single compute dispatch. It has an NVScaler mode (6-tap, 4 directional scaling + adaptive sharpening) and an NVSharpen sharpen-only mode. It targets DX11/DX12/Vulkan.
Reviewers find NIS and FSR 1 visually similar. NIS's stronger default sharpening is the main difference, and it looks almost identical to FSR when sharpening is lowered.

SGSR 1 is BSD-3-Clause. It is a single pass (12-tap Lanczos-like scaling + adaptive sharpening) that needs only one input texture and does not require AA input, though it works best with it. It costs about 0.30-0.48 ms on Snapdragon 888/8 Gen1/8 Gen2 at 1240x576 input, and Qualcomm calls its quality 'on par with other spatial upscalers'.

SGSR 2 is temporal (TAAU). It needs colour, D24S8 depth, velocity/motion vectors (dynamic objects) and a Halton jitterOffset. Variants are 2-pass-fs, 2-pass-cs and 3-pass-cs (GLSL); the 3-pass variant also takes opaque-only colour.
FSR 2 (MIT, HLSL CS_6_2 compiled to DX12/Vulkan backends) requires a render-resolution depth buffer, 2D motion vectors and sub-pixel jitter on all render-resolution inputs.
FSR 3.1 added Vulkan support (FidelityFX SDK 1.1) and still needs colour, depth, motion vectors, jitter and frame-time delta.

FSR 4 'requires an AMD 9000 series GPU or later', the FidelityFX API with signed binary distribution, and HLSL CS_6_4. Its inputs are colour, depth, motion vectors, jitter and frame-time delta. The docs give no guidance for running without motion vectors.

XeSS-SR is a temporal AI upscaler that replaces TAA. Minimum inputs per frame are jitter, input colour and dilated high-res motion vectors (or low-res motion vectors plus depth). It runs on Vulkan 1.1 (Intel Iris Xe+, or other vendors with specific features) and Windows 10/11 x64.
The XeSS SDK is under the Intel Simplified Software License: 'provided in binary form only', with no modification and no reverse engineering.

RPCS3 offers Output Scaling Mode {nearest, bilinear, fsr} and an RCAS sharpening intensity setting. The team refused DLSS because it 'requires per-object motion vectors, which we do not have' and said 'FSR is a spatial solution, which is ideal for us'.

Xenia offers postprocess_scaling_and_sharpening = bilinear/cas/fsr. It uses CAS when output is at or below native size and FSR for upscaling (EASU repeated in up-to-2x steps). Its blog notes it cannot recover softness when a game upscales internally.
Vita3K's Vulkan renderer has Nearest, Bilinear, Bicubic and FSR screen filters, with FSR using EASU and RCAS compute shaders.

Eden (yuzu descendant) offers ScalingFilter options NearestNeighbor, Bilinear, Bicubic, Gaussian, Lanczos, ScaleForce, Fsr, Area, ZeroTangent, BSpline, Mitchell, Spline1, Mmpx, Sgsr and SgsrEdge. yuzu introduced FSR in its Oct 2021 window-adapting filters.
Citron (yuzu fork) has an FSR filter, including an OpenGL FSR commit.
Ryujinx scaling filters are Bilinear, Nearest, FSR (with sharpening level) and Area; anti-aliasing options are FXAA and SMAA.
PPSSPP ships FSR-EASU (upscale) and FSR-RCAS (sharpen) as selectable post-processing shaders.
Dolphin offers output resampling modes Default, Bilinear, BSpline, MitchellNetravali, CatmullRom, SharpBilinear and AreaSampling, with no FSR.
Cemu has separate upscale/downscale filters (bilinear, bicubic, Hermite, nearest) and custom scaling shaders via graphic packs, with no built-in FSR.
ARMSX2 (PS2 emulator) added SGSR as a display upscaler alongside FSR 1.

AMD RSR is FSR-based in-driver upscaling. It requires 'desktop systems with discrete AMD Radeon RX 5000 Series Graphics and later, select AMD Advantage systems' with Adrenalin 22.7.1+. It is inactive until the game resolution is below native; in borderless fullscreen it lowers the desktop resolution automatically. It disables Radeon Image Sharpening and Integer Scaling.
NVIDIA driver NIS needs the game in fullscreen at a lower-than-native resolution, or the desktop resolution lowered as a workaround. Driver sharpening was extended to Vulkan/OpenGL in driver 441.41.
Intel's driver has no universal spatial upscaler, only retro/integer scaling. Intel's override (XeSS 3 multi-frame generation) applies only to games that already integrate XeSS 2.

Lossless Scaling (Steam, about $6.99) offers LS1, FSR, NIS, CAS and other scalers plus LSFG frame generation. It works as an overlay that requires windowed or borderless mode, not exclusive fullscreen.

Windows Auto SR does not support Vulkan, OpenGL or DX9 ('other graphics runtimes including DirectX 9, Vulkan, OpenGL are not supported'). It needs a Snapdragon X/X2 or Intel Core Ultra Series 3 Copilot+ PC, or a docked ROG Xbox Ally X.

This fork's 'Fullscreen' mode sets the window to the current desktop display mode, so the swapchain stays at native resolution and driver upscalers (RSR/NIS) will not trigger unless the desktop resolution is lowered.
Changing presenter or window size does not change guest rendering cost; guest GPU work is fixed by the game's own render targets (internal 3D resolution and 1080p video-out composition).

rep.implications:
1. **What to tell the owner.** The emulator already has FSR 1. It is AMD's original EASU+RCAS: spatial, MIT-licensed, two compute passes, the same version upstream shadPS4 uses. It works, but only when the game's video-out image is smaller than the window. For UFC 3/4 (1080p video-out) on a 1080p monitor it never activates. FSR 2, 3 and 4 are not present and cannot simply be dropped in.

2. **XeSS.** Adding XeSS is not realistic.
   - It is temporal and needs per-frame jitter, depth and motion vectors that the emulator does not have.
   - The motion vectors are not reliably available even if the game renders some internally: they would have to be found per game in the guest's GPU commands.
   - It is a closed binary DLL (Windows-only) whose license forbids modification.
   - Hooking a temporal upscaler in before the game's own 900p-to-1080p upscale would need per-title reverse engineering of render targets plus a jitter patch, with likely ghosting.
   - Fake inputs (zero motion vectors, no jitter) would leave XeSS or FSR 2 with no extra information, so the result would be roughly a blurred spatial upscale.

3. **Cheap, useful emulator-side improvements (inferences, ranked):**
   - **(a)** Add a sharpen-only path (AMD CAS, or RCAS alone) that runs when guest output is greater than or equal to the window. This counteracts the softness of the game's own upscale when the per-game patch lowers the 3D resolution to 720p or below. It is the Xenia approach, MIT, and costs well under 1 ms.
   - **(b)** Optionally offer NIS (MIT, GLSL provided) or SGSR 1 (BSD-3, one pass) as alternatives to FSR 1 for cases where the image is upscaled. They are similar in quality, and SGSR 1 is slightly cheaper.
   - **(c)** For real GPU savings, rely on the per-game internal-resolution patch:
     - 1600x900 to 1280x720 saves about 36% of the 3D pixels.
     - 960x540 saves about 64%.
     - If a patch can also shrink the video-out buffer itself, the presenter's FSR engages automatically on a 1080p window.

   A "lower presenter resolution + upscale" option on its own would not reduce GPU load and would only lose detail.

4. **What players can do today without emulator changes:**
   - **NVIDIA**: driver NIS, after lowering the desktop resolution.
   - **AMD discrete RX 5000+ desktops**: RSR (borderless works). Most AMD iGPU laptops are excluded.
   - **Intel Arc and anything else**: Lossless Scaling with the emulator in windowed or borderless mode. These mainly help when the window is smaller than the display.
   - **Windows Auto SR**: not an option. It does not support Vulkan.

- The exact version string is 'FSR 1 v1.20210629' (ffx_fsr1.h:6).

Faking zero motion vectors with no jitter gives smeared moving fighters, not just a 'blurred spatial upscale', which is a stronger risk than the report states (inference).
